messages.text:
You are implementing one GitHub issue in BrokkAi/bifrost-dev (the repository is cloned at `bifrost/`). Read `bifrost/AGENTS.md` first and follow it. In particular:

- Assign the issue to yourself and add the `agent-in-progress` label before starting (`gh issue edit N --add-assignee @me --add-label agent-in-progress`). Remove the label if you stand down without resolving it.
- Read the issue with all comments: `gh issue view N --comments`. The comments hold measurements and revised plans that override the issue body where they differ.
- `.agents/docs/*` files are point-in-time records; recheck any claim from them against the code before relying on it.
- Commit directly to `master`, only the files you changed, with a clear multiline message. Push to `origin/master`. If the push is rejected, `git fetch`, `git merge origin/master` (never rebase), rerun the affected tests, push again. If pushing is impossible (no credentials), leave your commits on the local branch and say so in your final message; do not open a PR.
- Build with plain `cargo`; do not set or redirect `CARGO_TARGET_DIR`. Keep validation proportional: `cargo fmt`, the two clippy commands from `.agents/docs/testing-and-rust-validation.md`, and `cargo nextest run --max-fail 100 -p <crate>` for the affected crates, with `BIFROST_PARALLELISM=1 RAYON_NUM_THREADS=1` and `JAVA_HOME` cleared. Run the whole test suite only if your change touches a shared path whose consumers extend beyond the crate.
- Other sessions are working concurrently on issues #3748, #3749, #3751, #3755, #3761, #3762, #3763, #3764 (and later #3754, #3756). Stay inside your issue's scope; do not refactor code those issues own. If you find a bug outside your scope, file an issue instead of fixing it.
- Check `nproc` and available memory first and size benchmark runs to the machine. Prefer existing `BIFROST_TIMING=1` spans and the MCP stdio server for measurements; the `benchmark/` harness is available too.
- You may delegate research, independent verification, or a second opinion on a design to your subagent, which runs a different model. Use it for review of your diff before you push.
- When done: comment on the issue with the landed commit SHA(s), what changed, exactly which validation ran, before/after measurements where the issue's acceptance asks for them, and any follow-ups. Close the issue only if its acceptance criteria are met; otherwise leave it open and state what remains. Finish with a short final message to me: outcome, commit, open questions. If you are blocked, stop and say so rather than widening scope.

Issue: #3749 (early cutoff on the update path). Plan step 1 already landed (34fa615c1). Your scope, in this order:

1. go.mod semantic digest (plan step 2 in the issue, about 3 s per require-only edit on kubernetes, measured in the comments). Parse `go.mod`; if the module path is unchanged, call the ordinary update path instead of `update_all`, and record the new byte digest. First check that Go dependency-pack consumers invalidate on `require` changes through their own keys. Extend the go.mod update test near `usages/get_definition/go.rs:7300-7330` with a require-only edit: assert no full reconcile and results equal to a fresh build. Land this as its own commit.

2. Incremental Rust crate derivation. The measurements show a fixed about 34 s to re-derive a large crate on any edit inside it (`collect_rows` 24 s, `export_declarations` 4 s, `import_resolution` 1.9 s, `root_references` 1.8 s, `publication` 1.7 s in `store/rust_crates.rs`), regardless of the edited file's size. Investigate whether `collect_rows` (first) can reuse per-file results for unchanged member blobs, keeping the crate rows identical to a fresh derivation. Use the existing `a_scoped_reconcile_publishes_what_the_full_pass_would` test as the model for an incremental-versus-fresh check. If a bounded implementation is feasible, implement it and measure a body edit inside `crates/bifrost-analysis` (a large crate) before and after, using an MCP session with the real watcher (write the edit, wait 2 s, issue a request); use a distinct literal per edit so the blob is new. If it is not feasible within the crate's design, write up why on the issue with the specific obstacle, and stop.

3. Do NOT implement plan step 4 (fragment-keyed usage graph). The measurements show the whole-workspace `usage_graph` is recomputed on every call, so there is no reusable graph to invalidate. Instead, post one comment on the issue summarizing whether the graph should become reusable across requests, as a question for the owner, with the tradeoff against the heap-residency rule in AGENTS.md.

Do not touch Cargo.toml manifest routing or digests (`needs_config_update_for`, `workspace_package_identity_input_digests`); that is #3754, which I will hand to you after this issue.
I'll start by reading the repo guidance, the issue with comments, and checking machine resources.
GitHub is not authenticated in this container: `gh` has no token and `git fetch` fails. I'll look for a local copy of the issue content before deciding how to proceed.
No local copy of the issue. The session that landed step 1 may have the issue text and measurements, so I'll search earlier sessions.
The measurement session is indexed. I'll pull the issue text and the go.mod and crate-derivation measurements from it.
I have enough background. Now the code, starting with the Go `update` path.
The Go `update` sends any `go.mod` change to `update_all`. Next I'll check how the store records package-identity inputs, and what the ordinary `update` does with a non-source file.
This is a broad question across several crates, so I'll hand the Go dependency-pack check to a child. Meanwhile I'll read the Rust crate derivation myself.
Two SELECTs in that stage do real joins: the root-references select and the unresolved-impl union. The rest are plain temp-table scans. Let me check which indexes the temp tables have.
No build exists yet. I'll start a release build in the background while I keep reading.
I'll give each collect_rows SELECT its own timing span before building, so one build answers which query dominates.
While the release build runs, I'll find how `BIFROST_TIMING` reports spans and which command gives a cold build.
The build is running. Now the profiling output format and the benchmark session helper.
I'll drive the server over stdio with a small Python script. First, the environment variable names for the watcher and the request budget.

Now the corpus: a clone of this repo at HEAD, kept outside the checkout.
While the build finishes, I'll read the existing go.mod update test the user pointed to.
The existing test covers a module-path change and an invalid manifest. For the require-only case I need a way to assert that no full reconcile ran. Let me look for an existing counter.
There is no counter for full rebuilds. I'll check for a parse or reconcile counter the test could use.
I'll decide the test observable after the child reports. Checking the build.
Status: I've settled the go.mod design and am about to implement it. First I'll check whether the release build has finished so the Rust baseline can run meanwhile.
Still compiling. rustc has already parsed the sources, so editing now won't change this baseline binary. Now the implementation: the adapter trait hook and the digest map.
I'll store both digests per input in the existing map, with a small struct as the value. Let me find the hash helper.
The update logic will compare identity digests. Before changing `TreeSitterAnalyzer::update`, I'll check how `RustAnalyzer::update` routes a Cargo.toml, so Rust behavior stays exactly as it is.
Now I'll make the edits: the adapter hook first, then the state field and its struct.
Now the consumers: content identity, the two overlay checks, and the two builders.
Now the core change in `TreeSitterAnalyzer::update`.
Now `GoAnalyzer::update`. The inner update decides escalation, so the wrapper only invalidates the nearest-module cache and delegates.
I'll also check that `MultiAnalyzer` delivers go.mod to `update` and not `update_all`.
The file already has test-only statics, so a test-only counter matches local practice. I'll make it thread-local so concurrent tests under plain `cargo test` don't interfere.
Now the test extension.
While the tests compile, I'll check the release build so the Rust baseline can start.
Nextest rejects `--max-fail` together with `--no-run`. I'll run the targeted Go tests directly, which builds the test binary as well.
While the tests build, I'll read the heap-residency section I need for the step 3 comment.
I'll confirm the fact behind the step 3 comment in code: that the whole-workspace usage graph is built per call with no cross-request cache.
The ranking graph has a `retained_bytes` method, which suggests something retains it. That matters for the step 3 comment, so I'll find out what.
Both builds are compiling `bifrost-analysis`, the largest crate. I'll load the Monitor tool and wait for the release binary.
While both builds run, I'll look at the existing plan pins for the crate-derivation statements. They show which collect_rows queries are already pinned.
While waiting, I'll draft the step 3 comment for the owner. GitHub is unreachable from this container, so drafts go to a file in the workspace.
I'll check the claim that `usage_graph` does not use the graph cache before relying on it.
Confirmed: only relevance uses the graph cache, and it has an "uncached, over budget" outcome, which supports the point about option 2. Now I'll wait for the builds.
The two Rust tests I expected to adjust. They compare the byte digest, so they now read the `content` field.
While the baseline runs, I'll get an independent review of the go.mod diff. Linting and the full test suite would compete with the benchmark for CPU, so they wait.
The baseline finished suspiciously fast. Checking why.
Meanwhile, the reviewer for the go.mod diff.
Mjolnir is not answering. I'll check whether the machine is overloaded.
The load average is 221 on 96 CPUs. Other sessions share this host, so wall-clock timings will be noisy, and I'll report them as such. I'll retry Mjolnir.
The reviewer was not created, so I'll spawn it again.
The reviewer found no correctness issues. It confirmed that the new test would have failed on the old code, where every go.mod change took `update_all`. Waiting for the release build.
Release build done. Starting the Rust baseline benchmark.
The cold build also derives every crate, so the log will show the per-statement collect_rows spans before any edit. I'll check the log for them.
While the cold build runs, I'll read the root-reference SQL to form a hypothesis ahead of the numbers.
The analysis crate comes in a later wave because it depends on the others. I'll wait for its spans.
Status: I found the 61 s cost. The root-references SELECT scans a materialized view once per reference. I'm replacing the view with an indexed temp table and pinning the new plan.
The cold build finished. Next I'll add the plan assertion and check the baseline edit results.
Now the plan pin, next to the trait-implementation pins.
The benchmark uses a copied binary, but compiling now would disturb its timings. I'll let the three baseline edits finish first.
While that runs, I'll copy the baseline store for the "after" run. The server has exited, so the copy is consistent.
The match was pgrep's own shell, not a server. Copying.
63 tests pass. I'll confirm the plan-pin test was among them, then start the "after" benchmark.
Both tests ran and passed. While the after benchmark runs, I'll hold off on heavy validation so it doesn't skew the comparison. Let me wait for the benchmark.
While validation runs, I'll draft the issue comment and the commit messages. GitHub is not reachable from this container, so the comment goes to a file.
Status: the first clippy command passed. The workspace-wide clippy is running, and the full test suites for the two crates run after it. Meanwhile I'll write both commit messages.
Both clippy commands pass, and the suites are at test 3,475 of 4,984. I'll wait for the finish.
One test failed, a build-lock timing test in blast radius. I'll read its failure and rerun it alone to see whether it comes from load or from my change.
It is recompiling. The earlier run built both crates together, so the feature set differs and this run gets a separate build. I'll wait for it.
My wait loop matches its own command line, which is the pgrep pitfall recorded in my notes, so it would never end. I'll stop it and read the rerun's output directly.
While it compiles, I'll read the failing test to judge whether my change could affect it.
Alone it passes in 2.1 s, so the earlier failure came from load. Validation is complete. Now the two commits, staging only my files.
Both commits are on local master. Next I'll try to push, though earlier fetches failed for lack of credentials.
Nothing in the issue overrides my work. Its revised order also matches what I did. Now I'll fetch and merge origin/master without rebasing, then check what changed near my files.
The merge is clean, and upstream touched none of my files. I'll check which crates it did change, so the retest covers what could interact.
Upstream rewrote part of `multi_analyzer.rs`, which routes go.mod to the Go analyzer. I'll check that the routing is intact.
All 51 pass on the merged tree. Pushing.
Pushed to origin/master. Now the issue comments. I'll fill in the commit SHAs and add the validation that ran.
I'll record two lasting facts in memory: the issue's outcome, since #3754 comes next, and the late-arriving GitHub token.

All three parts of #3749 are done. Both commits are pushed to master, and I left the issue open because the usage-graph question needs your decision.

**Commits** (merged into master as 8d434d4b3c):
- 6e9847e18c: a go.mod edit that keeps the module path is now an ordinary incremental update.
- 998d5c5e26: the Rust crate-derivation fix.

**1. go.mod digest.** I checked first that dependency packs don't depend on `update_all`: the MCP host already refreshes them for any changed go.mod.
- A new adapter hook reports what an input contributes to package identity. For Go that is the parsed module path.
- An edit that keeps it takes the ordinary update path and records the new byte digest, so content-keyed caches still move.
- Every other language, including Cargo.toml, keeps the old behavior. #3754 can plug a Cargo.toml digest into this same hook.
- The extended test asserts that a require-only edit runs no full rebuild and matches a fresh build. A reviewer confirmed it would have failed on the old code.
- I did not re-measure the kubernetes edit; the issue's figure is about 3 s before the change.

**2. Rust crate derivation.** The fixed ~34 s was not per-file work. It was one bad query plan: the root-references SELECT scanned a temp view once per reference, 177,237 references against about 2,200 modules. That view is now a keyed temp table, and a plan pin guards it.

Measured with the real watcher, a body edit in `crates/bifrost-analysis`, 3 edits each:

| | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Request after the edit | 91–102 s | 25–28 s |
| That one SELECT | 62–70 s | 0.7–0.9 s |

- **Rows unchanged:** all 239,694 crate rows were identical between the old and new code's derivations of the same crate.
- **Noisy host:** other sessions pushed the load average to about 220 on 96 CPUs, so absolute times are inflated. The before and after runs were back to back.
- **Per-file reuse:** I did not attempt it for the remaining ~25 s, because it would need a schema redesign. The issue comment gives the specific obstacles.

**3. Usage graph.** I posted the question on the issue, with a recommendation. Keep `usage_graph` per request for now. If reuse is ever needed, store per-file edge fragments as rows in SQLite, since a large retained graph in memory would break the heap-residency rule.

**Validation:**
- `cargo fmt` and both clippy commands are clean.
- The full test suites for `brokk-bifrost-analysis` and `brokk-bifrost-go` passed 4,983 of 4,984. The one failure is a wall-clock test on a Python workspace that failed under the load and passed alone.
- The affected tests passed again after merging origin/master.

**Setup note:** GitHub credentials only appeared partway through the session. So I claimed the issue and read its comments late, after most of the work; nothing in them conflicted with it. I have removed the in-progress label and my assignment.

The edit benchmark script is `/workspace/dda8433492d9e3e31df618dce5b5d690/bench/edit_bench.py`, outside the repo and not committed.

No comments on the issue; the user's brief matches its plan. Next I'll read how `store/rust_crates.rs` parses manifests for crate topology, since the brief asks me to reuse that parser.
